title: Using a Thesaurus to Choose Words
keyIdea: A thesaurus gives synonyms: words with a similar meaning, not the same meaning. To choose well, first find the sense of the headword that matches your sentence (bright can mean shining or clever). Then check three things: the feeling the word carries (slim is kind, skinny is not), its strength (warm, hot, scorching), and whether it suits the setting (purchase in a letter, grab in a chat). Read the sentence with the new word in it; if it sounds wrong or you are not sure what the word means, check a dictionary or keep your first word.
familyTip: Next time your child writes nice, good or said, open a thesaurus together (a book or an online one) and read out the list. Ask: which of these fits our sentence, and which would sound odd? Try one odd one aloud and laugh at it.

visual.caption: Does the synonym fit this sentence: “It was a nice, warm day for a picnic”? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pick the sense, place synonyms from kind to unkind, order by strength, sort formal and chatty words, and let clues pick a verb.

kid: A thesaurus is a book or website of synonyms. Synonyms are words with a similar meaning. You look up a word, called the headword, and it gives you a list of other words to try.
Similar is not the same. Some headwords have more than one sense. Bright can mean shining, like the sun. It can also mean clever, like a pupil. Pick the list that matches your sentence.

Synonyms can also carry a feeling. Slim and skinny both mean thin. Slim sounds kind, but skinny can sound rude. They can also differ in strength: hot is more than warm, and scorching is more than hot.
Last, think about who will read it. Purchase is good in a letter to the head. Grab is fine in a chat with a friend. Read your sentence aloud with the new word. If it sounds wrong, try another one.
adult: Ages 10 to 11. In England this is the Years 5 and 6 programme: pupils use a thesaurus, and when writing they select vocabulary, understanding how such choices can change and enhance meaning, including the difference between formal and informal vocabulary. In the US it matches Common Core L.4.5c and L.5.5c (relating words to synonyms with similar but not identical meanings) and L.5.4c (consulting reference materials to clarify the precise meaning of a word).

A thesaurus entry is organised by headword, word class and sense: one headword such as bright or cool can have several numbered sense groups, each with its own synonyms. Synonyms within a group still differ in connotation (the feelings and judgements a word carries), in intensity (warm, hot, scorching) and in register (formal purchase and assist, informal grab and give a hand).

A good choice is the word that fits the sense, the feeling, the strength and the reader. Context in the sentence often settles it: an exclamation mark and a warning suggest shouted, and a sleeping baby suggests whispered. When a synonym is unfamiliar, a dictionary check before using it is part of the skill.

Common mistakes: taking the first or the longest word on the list; choosing from the wrong sense (a dazzling pupil); ignoring connotation (calling a friend scrawny); picking a word that is too strong or too weak (furious when someone is a little cross); using chatty words in formal writing; and swapping every repeated word, so the writing becomes forced. In the lab your child practises each of these checks.

practice.prompt: Which word could replace bright in: “The bright stars shone all night”?
practice.hint: Is the sentence about light or about being clever?
practice.explain: Stars give off light, so the shining sense fits: gleaming. Clever and smart belong to the other sense of bright.

practice.prompt: Mia finds {n} synonyms for thin. Which one is the kindest way to describe her dad?
practice.hint: Which word sounds like praise rather than a worry?
practice.explain: Slender means thin in a graceful, pleasant way. Bony and scrawny carry an unkind feeling, as if he is too thin.

practice.prompt: Put these in order, weakest first: furious, annoyed, angry.
practice.hint: Which word is only a little cross? Start there.
practice.explain: Annoyed is a little cross, angry is more, and furious is very angry. They are synonyms of different strength.

practice.prompt: Leo has {n} words to choose from for a letter to the head teacher. Which fits: “Could you ___ us with the fair?”
practice.hint: Which choice is formal enough for a letter?
practice.explain: Assist is formal, so it suits a letter to the head. Give us a hand and help us out a bit are chatty phrases for friends.

practice.hint: Look for a clue about how loud he would speak.
practice.explain: A sleeping baby means Dad speaks very quietly, so whispered fits. Yelled is loud and announced is said out to a group.

choices: a word with a similar meaning
a word with the opposite meaning
a word that sounds the same
pool.hint: Think about what a thesaurus gives you when you look up a word.
pool.explain: A synonym has a similar meaning, like big and large. An opposite is an antonym, and a word that sounds the same is a homophone.

pool.prompt: The thesaurus lists cool: 1 chilly, chilled; 2 calm, relaxed. Which fits: “Stay cool in the exam”?
pool.hint: Is the sentence about temperature or about feelings?
pool.explain: Staying cool in an exam means staying calm, so pick from sense 2. Chilled and chilly are about temperature.

pool.prompt: Why is “The scorching day was nice for a walk” an odd sentence?
choices: Scorching is too strong: it means very, very hot
Scorching is the wrong word class
pool.hint: How hot is scorching compared with warm?
pool.explain: Scorching means extremely hot, which is not nice for a walk. Warm or sunny would be the right strength.

pool.prompt: The park needs {n} new benches. Which word suits a formal letter: “We wish to ___ {n} benches”?
pool.hint: Which word would sound right in a letter to the council?
pool.explain: Purchase is formal and means buy. Grab and snap up are chatty and belong in a talk with friends.

pool.prompt: Ben swaps said for exclaimed in all {n} lines of his story. What goes wrong?
choices: Exclaimed means saying with surprise, so it does not fit every line
Exclaimed is not a real word
Nothing: more different words is always better
pool.hint: Does every line in a story have surprise in it?
pool.explain: Each synonym has its own meaning. Exclaimed only fits a surprised or excited line, so swapping every said makes the story sound forced.

pool.prompt: Which word gives the most negative feeling about a small house?
pool.hint: Which word suggests the house is too small?
pool.explain: Poky suggests a small house that feels cramped and unpleasant. Cosy is warm and friendly, and compact is neutral, even positive.

pool.prompt: You find the word “jubilant” in a thesaurus but do not know it. What should you do?
choices: Check its meaning in a dictionary before using it
Use it, because long words are better
Use it, because all words on the list mean the same
pool.hint: What could go wrong if you use a word you do not know?
pool.explain: Check a new word in a dictionary first. Jubilant means very happy and proud, which fits some sentences but not others.

pool.prompt: “Please, can I have some water?” Zoe ___ politely.
pool.explain: Please and politely show a gentle request, so asked fits. Demanded and snapped are rude and would not match politely.
